claim: Four-jointed acts on Fat to promote its binding to Dachsous in vivo
source: We demonstrate that in vivo, Four-jointed acts both on Fat to promote its binding to Dachsous and on Dachsous to inhibit its binding to Fat, with a bias towards a stronger effect on Fat.
evidence: Supported by FRAP experiments showing reduced Ft-EGFP stability in fj mutants and phosphomutant analyses

claim: Four-jointed acts on Dachsous to inhibit its binding to Fat in vivo
source: We demonstrate that in vivo, Four-jointed acts both on Fat to promote its binding to Dachsous and on Dachsous to inhibit its binding to Fat, with a bias towards a stronger effect on Fat.
evidence: Supported by FRAP experiments with Ds phosphomutants showing increased stability when phosphorylation sites are blocked

claim: Four-jointed has a stronger effect on Fat than on Dachsous
source: We demonstrate that in vivo, Four-jointed acts both on Fat to promote its binding to Dachsous and on Dachsous to inhibit its binding to Fat, with a bias towards a stronger effect on Fat.
evidence: Supported by FRAP data showing that removal of Fj results in net loss of Ft-Ds binding stability, indicating dominant effect on Ft

claim: Opposing gradients of Fat and Dachsous phosphorylation are sufficient to explain the observed pattern of Fat–Dachsous binding and planar polarisation across the wing
source: Overall, we show that opposing gradients of Fat and Dachsous phosphorylation are sufficient to explain the observed pattern of Fat–Dachsous binding and planar polarisation across the wing, and thus demonstrate the mechanism by which a long-range gradient is interpreted.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling combined with experimental FRAP data across the Fj gradient

claim: Fat and Dachsous are large atypical cadherins that bind to each other heterophilically
source: Ft and Ds are large atypical cadherins known to bind to each other heterophilically (Ma et al., 2003; Matakatsu and Blair, 2004)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Four-jointed is a kinase active in the Golgi
source: Fj is a kinase shown to be active in the Golgi (Strutt et al., 2004; Ishikawa et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Complementary graded expression patterns of Dachsous and Four-jointed result in planar polarisation of Fat and Dachsous across cells
source: Complementary graded expression patterns of Ds and Fj (Zeidler et al., 1999, 2000; Yang et al., 2002; Ma et al., 2003) result in the planar polarisation of Ft and Ds across cells, with (in the developing wing) Ds accumulating distally and Ft accumulating proximally (Ambegaonkar et al., 2012; Bosveld et al., 2012; Brittle et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple previous studies

claim: In the developing wing, Dachsous accumulates distally and Fat accumulates proximally
source: Complementary graded expression patterns of Ds and Fj (Zeidler et al., 1999, 2000; Yang et al., 2002; Ma et al., 2003) result in the planar polarisation of Ft and Ds across cells, with (in the developing wing) Ds accumulating distally and Ft accumulating proximally (Ambegaonkar et al., 2012; Bosveld et al., 2012; Brittle et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Four-jointed can phosphorylate several cadherin repeats of both Fat and Dachsous
source: Fj is able to phosphorylate several cadherin repeats of both Ft and Ds (Ishikawa et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Four-jointed acts on three serines in Dachsous to inhibit the binding of Dachsous to Fat in vitro
source: Using a cell aggregation assay, based on Drosophila S2 cells co-transfected with Fj, Ds, or Ft, Brittle et al. (2010) deduced that Fj was able to act on three previously identified serines in Ds to inhibit the binding of Ds to Ft (Ishikawa et al., 2008; Brittle et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous in vitro study

claim: Four-jointed inhibits the ability of Dachsous to bind to Fat in an alkaline phosphatase-based cell surface binding assay
source: Using an alkaline phosphatase-based cell surface binding assay, Simon et al. (2010) similarly found that Fj inhibited the ability of Ds to bind to Ft and were also able to demonstrate an improvement in Ft binding to Ds.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous in vitro study

claim: Four-jointed improves Fat binding to Dachsous in an alkaline phosphatase-based cell surface binding assay
source: Using an alkaline phosphatase-based cell surface binding assay, Simon et al. (2010) similarly found that Fj inhibited the ability of Ds to bind to Ft and were also able to demonstrate an improvement in Ft binding to Ds.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous in vitro study

claim: Over-expressed Four-jointed promotes Fat activity and inhibits Dachsous activity in vivo
source: In addition, in vivo assays examining the propagation of polarity from over-expression clones also found that over-expressed Fj promoted Ft activity and inhibited Ds activity (Brittle et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: A gradient of 2.5–3.5% Four-jointed expression between adjacent cells was observed along the proximo-distal axis in Drosophila larval wing discs
source: A gradient of 2.5–3.5% between adjacent cells (Figure 1B) was observed along the proximo-distal axis.
evidence: Supported by measurements from wing disc images with fj null clones for background correction

claim: If Four-jointed acts on Dachsous only, weak asymmetry is seen within cells (3.8% increase) and a tissue gradient of higher to lower Ft–Ds binding is seen as Fj increases
source: If Fj acts on Ds only (D and E), weak asymmetry is seen within cells (3.8% increase) and a tissue gradient of higher to lower Ft–Ds binding is seen as Fj increases.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 1D and E

claim: If Four-jointed acts on Fat only, weak asymmetry is seen within cells (3.6% increase) and a tissue gradient of lower to higher Ft–Ds binding is observed as Fj increases
source: If Fj acts on Ft only (D′ and E′) similar weak asymmetry (3.6% increase) is seen within cells, however, a tissue gradient of lower to higher Ft–Ds binding is observed as Fj increases.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 1D′ and E′

claim: If Four-jointed acts on both Fat and Dachsous, stronger asymmetry is seen within cells (7.9% increase) and the tissue gradient is much reduced
source: If Fj can act on both Ft and Ds (D″ and E″) stronger asymmetry is seen within cells (7.9% increase) and the tissue gradient is much reduced.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 1D″ and E″

claim: Addition of an EGFP tag does not affect Dachsous protein localisation
source: Wing discs containing clones of (A) ds-EGFP/+ and (B) ft-EGFP/+ labelled for EGFP (green) and Ds or Ft, respectively (red), show that addition of an EGFP tag does not affect protein localisation.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images showing similar localization patterns

claim: Addition of an EGFP tag does not affect Fat protein localisation
source: Wing discs containing clones of (A) ds-EGFP/+ and (B) ft-EGFP/+ labelled for EGFP (green) and Ds or Ft, respectively (red), show that addition of an EGFP tag does not affect protein localisation.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images showing similar localization patterns

claim: Expression levels of tagged Dachsous-EGFP are similar to wild-type Dachsous
source: Quantification of (A′) Ds or (B′) Ft junctional protein confirms expression levels of tagged proteins are similar to wild-type.
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2A′

claim: Expression levels of tagged Fat-EGFP are similar to wild-type Fat
source: Quantification of (A′) Ds or (B′) Ft junctional protein confirms expression levels of tagged proteins are similar to wild-type.
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2B′

claim: Dachsous-EGFP has a large stable fraction of protein in puncta
source: FRAP analysis of (C) Ds-EGFP and (D) Ft-EGFP puncta (bright regions, solid line) and non-puncta (dashed line) reveals a large stable fraction of protein in puncta
evidence: Supported by FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Fat-EGFP has a large stable fraction of protein in puncta
source: FRAP analysis of (C) Ds-EGFP and (D) Ft-EGFP puncta (bright regions, solid line) and non-puncta (dashed line) reveals a large stable fraction of protein in puncta
evidence: Supported by FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: There is a large significant difference in stable amount of Dachsous-EGFP between puncta and non-puncta regions (p = 0.0001)
source: Multiplying the intensity of FRAP regions prior to bleaching (C′ and D′) by the stable fraction plateau (C and D) reveals a final 'stable amount' of protein at junctions (C″ and D″) and a large significant difference between puncta and non-puncta regions (both p = 0.0001, error bars denote standard error (SEM) here and in all remaining figures).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of FRAP data shown in Figure 2C″

claim: There is a large significant difference in stable amount of Fat-EGFP between puncta and non-puncta regions (p = 0.0001)
source: Multiplying the intensity of FRAP regions prior to bleaching (C′ and D′) by the stable fraction plateau (C and D) reveals a final 'stable amount' of protein at junctions (C″ and D″) and a large significant difference between puncta and non-puncta regions (both p = 0.0001, error bars denote standard error (SEM) here and in all remaining figures).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of FRAP data shown in Figure 2D″

claim: Fat puncta persist over time during antibody internalisation assay
source: Apical confocal sections of a V5-Ft antibody internalisation assay in pre-pupal wing, with time points of 0, 10, and 20 min, reveal persistent Ft puncta over time while quantification of total apical levels (right panel) shows protein internalisation is occurring (p = 0.01 at 10 min and p = 0.001 at 20 min)
evidence: Supported by time-course imaging data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Total apical Fat levels decrease during antibody internalisation assay (p = 0.01 at 10 min and p = 0.001 at 20 min)
source: Apical confocal sections of a V5-Ft antibody internalisation assay in pre-pupal wing, with time points of 0, 10, and 20 min, reveal persistent Ft puncta over time while quantification of total apical levels (right panel) shows protein internalisation is occurring (p = 0.01 at 10 min and p = 0.001 at 20 min)
evidence: Supported by quantification of imaging data shown in Figure 2E

claim: V5-Fat previously at the cell surface is seen in discrete intracellular puncta at t = 20 where it co-localises with early endosome marker Hrs
source: Sub-apical confocal sections of pre-pupal wing show V5-Ft previously at the cell surface is seen in discrete intracellular puncta at t = 20, where it co-localises with early endosome marker Hrs (magenta) (F′), confirming antibody internalisation rather than antibody drop off.
evidence: Supported by co-localization imaging data shown in Figure 2F and F′

claim: Dachsous-EGFP in ftG-rv clones results in more rapid and increased protein recovery during FRAP
source: FRAP analysis of Ds-EGFP in ftG-rv clones (G) and Ft-EGFP in a dsUA071 background (H) resulted in more rapid and increased protein recovery.
evidence: Supported by FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 2G

claim: Fat-EGFP in a dsUA071 background results in more rapid and increased protein recovery during FRAP
source: FRAP analysis of Ds-EGFP in ftG-rv clones (G) and Ft-EGFP in a dsUA071 background (H) resulted in more rapid and increased protein recovery.
evidence: Supported by FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 2H

claim: Dachsous-EGFP shows a loss of puncta and diffuse distribution when Fat is not present
source: Live images of Ds-EGFP (I) and Ds-EGFP with a ftG-rv clone (I′; blue dots indicate first row of mutant cells) show a loss of puncta and diffuse distribution of Ds-EGFP when Ft is not present.
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 2I and I′

claim: Fat-EGFP shows a loss of puncta and diffuse distribution in a dsUA071 mutant
source: Similar distribution of Ft-EGFP (J) is seen in a dsUA071 mutant (J′).
evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 2J and J′

claim: There is almost twice as much Fat-EGFP as Dachsous-EGFP in puncta regions (p = 0.01)
source: Comparison of Ds-EGFP and Ft-EGFP protein levels taken at the same confocal settings suggests there is almost twice as much Ft-EGFP (n = 4 wings) as Ds-EGFP (n = 2 wings) in puncta regions (p = 0.01).
evidence: Supported by quantitative comparison shown in Figure 2K

claim: Both Fat-EGFP and Dachsous-EGFP mobile fractions exhibit slower recovery in puncta compared to non-puncta and mutants
source: Bar chart representing time taken for 50% protein recovery to occur during FRAP experiments. Both Ft-EGFP and Ds-EGFP mobile fractions exhibit slower recovery in puncta compared to non-puncta and mutants.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2L

claim: The observed stability of Dachsous is dependent on the presence of Fat
source: Removal of the putative binding partner resulted in the loss of obvious puncta and the almost complete recovery of fluorescence after bleaching, indicating that the majority of protein had become unstable at junctions. Thus, the observed stability of each protein is dependent on the presence of the binding partner.
evidence: Supported by FRAP experiments in ft mutant backgrounds

claim: The observed stability of Fat is dependent on the presence of Dachsous
source: Removal of the putative binding partner resulted in the loss of obvious puncta and the almost complete recovery of fluorescence after bleaching, indicating that the majority of protein had become unstable at junctions. Thus, the observed stability of each protein is dependent on the presence of the binding partner.
evidence: Supported by FRAP experiments in ds mutant backgrounds

claim: Mobile populations of Dachsous-EGFP show slower movement in the presence of Fat compared to that in the absence of Fat
source: Comparing data for the rate of recovery of fluorescence of Ds-EGFP (Table 1 and Figure 2L) further revealed that the mobile populations of Ds-EGFP show slower movement, either in puncta or non-puncta, in the presence of Ft, compared to that in the absence of Ft (where no puncta are observed).
evidence: Supported by rate analysis from FRAP data shown in Table 1 and Figure 2L

claim: There is a mobile population of Dachsous-EGFP bound to Fat present in both puncta and non-puncta regions which shows less rapid movement than free Dachsous-EGFP
source: This suggests that in addition to the immobile population of Ds bound to Ft which is concentrated in puncta as described in the previous section, there is also a mobile population of Ds-EGFP present in both puncta and non-puncta regions which is bound to Ft and shows less rapid movement than free Ds-EGFP (i.e., Ds-EGFP in the absence of Ft).
evidence: Inferred from FRAP rate data comparing presence and absence of Ft

claim: The reduction in the rate of movement of mobile Dachsous-Ft heterodimers in puncta as opposed to non-puncta might indicate the presence of a cis-dimerisation mechanism that promotes the clustering of heterodimers into the puncta
source: The reduction in the rate of movement of these mobile Ds-Ft heterodimers in puncta as opposed to non-puncta might indicate the presence of a cis-dimerisation mechanism that promotes the clustering of heterodimers into the puncta.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of differential mobility rates

claim: Mechanisms such as physical interactions with the cytoskeleton similar to those seen for E-Cadherin clustering may be responsible for the reduced mobility of Dachsous-Fat heterodimers in puncta
source: Alternatively, mechanisms such as physical interactions with the cytoskeleton similar to those seen for E-Cadherin clustering (Cavey et al., 2008) may be responsible for the reduced mobility.
evidence: Speculative interpretation with citation to analogous mechanism

claim: There is a negligible difference in the rate of movement of Fat-EGFP in non-punctate regions in the presence of Dachsous as compared to the rate of movement of Fat-EGFP in the absence of Dachsous
source: However, in this case there is a negligible difference in the rate of movement of Ft-EGFP in non-punctate regions in the presence of Ds, as compared to the rate of movement of Ft-EGFP in the absence of Ds, and also a faster rate of Ft-EGFP mobility within puncta as compared to Ds-EGFP in puncta.
evidence: Supported by rate analysis from FRAP data in Table 1

claim: Fat-EGFP shows a faster rate of mobility within puncta as compared to Dachsous-EGFP in puncta
source: However, in this case there is a negligible difference in the rate of movement of Ft-EGFP in non-punctate regions in the presence of Ds, as compared to the rate of movement of Ft-EGFP in the absence of Ds, and also a faster rate of Ft-EGFP mobility within puncta as compared to Ds-EGFP in puncta.
evidence: Supported by rate analysis from FRAP data in Table 1

claim: The differences in Fat-EGFP mobility rates are due to there being an excess of Fat-EGFP present over Dachsous, resulting in an increased proportion of the population of Fat-EGFP being unbound and thereby free to move into bleached regions
source: We surmise that these differences are due to there being an excess of Ft-EGFP present over Ds (see Figure 2K), resulting in an increased proportion of the population of Ft-EGFP being unbound and thereby free to move into bleached regions.
evidence: Inferred from protein level measurements and mobility data

claim: Fat and Dachsous bind to each other across cell membranes resulting in the production of immobile fractions of Fat and Dachsous at cell junctions
source: Overall, we conclude from our FRAP experiments using 'wild-type' Ft-EGFP and Ds-EGFP, that Ft and Ds bind to each other across cell membranes resulting in the production of immobile fractions of Ft and Ds at cell junctions, and a reduction in mobility of Ft and Ds at junctions.
evidence: Concluded from FRAP experiments showing stable fractions dependent on binding partner

claim: Fat-Dachsous binding results in a reduction in mobility of Fat and Dachsous at junctions
source: Overall, we conclude from our FRAP experiments using 'wild-type' Ft-EGFP and Ds-EGFP, that Ft and Ds bind to each other across cell membranes resulting in the production of immobile fractions of Ft and Ds at cell junctions, and a reduction in mobility of Ft and Ds at junctions.
evidence: Concluded from FRAP experiments showing reduced mobility in presence of binding partner

claim: Dachsous-EGFP becomes less stable upon removal of Four-jointed (p = 0.004)
source: However, we found that Ds-EGFP became less stable upon removal of Fj (Figure 3A″, p = 0.004), with a reduction in both the stable fraction (i.e., an increase in the height of the plateau) and the stable amount at junctions (Figure 3A,A″).
evidence: Supported by FRAP data in fj mutant background shown in Figure 3A and A″

claim: Fat-EGFP shows a reduction in stable fraction and stable amount at junctions in a fj background (p = 0.04)
source: In this case analysis of Ft-EGFP recovery in a fj background did result in a reduction in stable fraction and stable amount at junctions (Figure 3B,B″, p = 0.04).
evidence: Supported by FRAP data in fj mutant background shown in Figure 3B and B″

claim: The half time rate of recovery of Fat-EGFP and Dachsous-EGFP is decreased in the absence of Four-jointed
source: The half time rate of recovery of Ft-EGFP and Ds-EGFP was also decreased in the absence of Fj, consistent with a reduction of binding affinity allowing more rapid mobility (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by rate analysis from FRAP data shown in Table 1

claim: The overall result of removing Four-jointed is a reduction in stability of the Fat–Dachsous dimer
source: Thus, the overall result of removing Fj was a reduction in stability of the Ft–Ds dimer.
evidence: Concluded from FRAP experiments in fj mutant backgrounds

claim: The effect Four-jointed has on Fat is dominant to any effect it might have on Dachsous in the wing disc
source: A loss of stability, rather than a gain, suggests that, at least in the wing disc, the effect Fj has on Ft is dominant to any which it might have on Ds.
evidence: Inferred from net loss of stability when Fj is removed

claim: Mutating the phosphorylation sites in Dachsous to prevent Four-jointed phosphorylation results in a strong increase in the amount of stable protein (p = 0.0004)
source: When comparing the stability of 'wild-type' Ds-EGFP (expressed from the Act-ds-EGFP transgene) and a form of Ds with the phosphorylation sites mutated to alanine to block phosphorylation (Act-ds-S>Ax3-EGFP; Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), there was a strong increase in the amount of stable protein present in the mutant (Figure 4A″, 196.3 ± 18 and 428.9 ± 35 intensity units respectively, p = 0.0004).
evidence: Supported by FRAP data comparing wild-type and phosphomutant Ds shown in Figure 4A and A″

claim: The increase in stable Dachsous in the phosphomutant is solely due to the inability of Four-jointed to phosphorylate Dachsous
source: As Fj was still expressed and presumably able to act normally on Ft in this experiment, the increase in stable amount must be solely due to the inability of Fj to phosphorylate Ds.
evidence: Inferred from experimental design where only Ds phosphorylation is blocked

claim: Additional loss of Four-jointed from the Dachsous phosphomutant background results in a decrease in stability back to a level similar to wild-type
source: Additional loss of Fj, to remove potential Ft phosphorylation from the experiment, resulted in the expected decrease in stability, back to a level similar to 'wild-type' (Figure 4B,E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 4B and E

claim: The effect of Four-jointed on Fat is dominant to that on Dachsous, as confirmed by phosphomutant experiments
source: Additional loss of Fj, to remove potential Ft phosphorylation from the experiment, resulted in the expected decrease in stability, back to a level similar to 'wild-type' (Figure 4B,E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), again consistent with the effect of Fj on Ft being dominant to that on Ds.
evidence: Inferred from phosphomutant experiments showing loss of Ds phosphomutant advantage when Fj is removed

claim: Fat phosphomutant (Act-ft-S/T>Ax5-EGFP) shows a decreased stable fraction and a large reduction in stable amount when compared to wild-type (p = 0.006)
source: Consistent with previous results, a Ft phosphomutant (Act-ft-S/T>Ax5-EGFP) showed a decreased stable fraction (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and a large reduction in stable amount when compared to 'wild-type' (Figure 4C″, 97.9 ± 15 and 194.5 ± 24 intensity units respectively, p = 0.006).
evidence: Supported by FRAP data comparing wild-type and phosphomutant Ft shown in Figure 4C and C″

claim: Removal of Four-jointed from the Fat phosphomutant background does not result in a significant change in stable amount at the junctions
source: Removal of Fj, and therefore Ds phosphorylation, from the phosphomutant background (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) did not result in a significant change in stable amount at the junctions
evidence: Supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 4D

claim: The observed reduction in stability of the Fat phosphomutant is primarily due to a loss of Four-jointed phosphorylation of Fat
source: Removal of Fj, and therefore Ds phosphorylation, from the phosphomutant background (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) did not result in a significant change in stable amount at the junctions confirming that the observed reduction in stability of the phosphomutant (Figure 4C″) was primarily due to a loss of Fj phosphorylation of Ft.
evidence: Inferred from lack of change when Fj is removed from Ft phosphomutant background

claim: Phosphomutant experiments reveal in vivo effects of Four-jointed phosphorylation on both Fat and Dachsous
source: Importantly, the phosphomutant experiments have revealed in vivo affects of Fj phosphorylation on both Ft and Ds.
evidence: Concluded from phosphomutant FRAP experiments

claim: Mutating the Dachsous phosphorylation sites results in a significantly improved binding ability
source: Mutating the Ds phosphorylation sites resulted in a significantly improved binding ability, however, this improved ability was lost when Ft was also not phosphorylated.
evidence: Supported by FRAP data from Ds phosphomutant experiments

claim: The improved binding ability of Dachsous phosphomutant is lost when Fat is also not phosphorylated
source: Mutating the Ds phosphorylation sites resulted in a significantly improved binding ability, however, this improved ability was lost when Ft was also not phosphorylated.
evidence: Supported by FRAP data comparing Ds phosphomutant with and without Fj

claim: Phosphomutant experiments confirm there is a dominant effect of Four-jointed phosphorylation on Fat
source: Additionally, the phosphomutant experiments have confirmed that there is a dominant effect of Fj phosphorylation on Ft.
evidence: Concluded from phosphomutant FRAP experiments

claim: When Four-jointed acts on both Dachsous and Fat with a Ft bias, a cellular asymmetry of 4.1% is observed in the computational model
source: When Fj can act on both Ft and Ds with a Ft bias, an intermediate outcome between acting on Ft only and acting on Ft and Ds without a bias is seen and a cellular asymmetry of 4.1% is observed.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 5A

claim: A tissue gradient of 4.7% is observed in the computational model when Four-jointed acts on both Fat and Dachsous with a Ft bias, compared to 10% when Fj acts on Ft alone
source: A tissue gradient of 4.7% in the model when acting on both Ft and Ds, compared to 10% when Fj acts on Ft alone (Figure 1D′,E′) suggests that Ds phosphorylation is required to counter the strong graded effects of Ft phosphorylation.
evidence: Supported by computational modeling results comparing different scenarios

claim: Dachsous phosphorylation is required to counter the strong graded effects of Fat phosphorylation
source: A tissue gradient of 4.7% in the model when acting on both Ft and Ds, compared to 10% when Fj acts on Ft alone (Figure 1D′,E′) suggests that Ds phosphorylation is required to counter the strong graded effects of Ft phosphorylation.
evidence: Inferred from computational modeling comparing tissue gradients in different scenarios

claim: Endogenously expressed Dachsous-EGFP shows a larger stable fraction in regions of high Four-jointed (distal)
source: FRAP analysis of endogenously expressed Ds-EGFP reveals a larger stable fraction in regions of high Fj (distal) despite showing slightly less overall fluorescence (B′).
evidence: Supported by FRAP data comparing proximal and distal regions shown in Figure 5B

claim: A significantly increased stable amount of Dachsous-EGFP is seen in high Four-jointed regions (p = 0.01, 23% difference)
source: Overall, a significantly increased stable amount is seen in high Fj regions (B″ p = 0.01, 23% difference).
evidence: Supported by quantitative FRAP analysis shown in Figure 5B″

claim: The difference in stable Dachsous-EGFP amount between high and low Four-jointed regions is lost in a fj mutant
source: FRAP analysis in a fj mutant shows that this difference is lost when taking pre-bleach intensity levels into account (C′, C″).
evidence: Supported by FRAP data in fj mutant shown in Figure 5C′ and C″

claim: A greater difference in stable Dachsous-S>Ax3-EGFP at junctions is observed between high and low Four-jointed regions (p = 0.01, 53% difference)
source: Despite relatively small differences between stable fractions (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), we saw a greater difference in stable Ds-S>Ax3-EGFP at junctions between high and low Fj regions (Figure 5E″, 109.2 ± 21 proximally and 230.4 ± 37 distally p = 0.01, 53% difference)
evidence: Supported by FRAP data with Ds phosphomutant shown in Figure 5E″

claim: The difference in stable Dachsous-S>Ax3-EGFP between high and low Four-jointed regions is lost upon removal of Fj
source: which was again lost upon removal of Fj (Figure 5F″, 97.8 ± 9 proximally and 78.2 ± 25 distally, NS).
evidence: Supported by FRAP data in fj mutant background shown in Figure 5F″

claim: A slight gradient of Fat-Dachsous binding strength exists across the tissue
source: These results directly confirm the predictions of the model, showing not only that a slight gradient of binding strength exists across the tissue, but also that an opposing gradient of Ds phosphorylation usually acts to counter the effects of a gradient of Ft phosphorylation, resulting in a relatively even distribution of bound Ft–Ds complexes at junctions across the tissue axis from low to high Fj.
evidence: Supported by FRAP experiments across the Fj gradient

claim: An opposing gradient of Dachsous phosphorylation acts to counter the effects of a gradient of Fat phosphorylation
source: These results directly confirm the predictions of the model, showing not only that a slight gradient of binding strength exists across the tissue, but also that an opposing gradient of Ds phosphorylation usually acts to counter the effects of a gradient of Ft phosphorylation, resulting in a relatively even distribution of bound Ft–Ds complexes at junctions across the tissue axis from low to high Fj.
evidence: Supported by FRAP experiments comparing wild-type and phosphomutants across the Fj gradient

claim: Opposing gradients of Dachsous and Fat phosphorylation result in a relatively even distribution of bound Fat–Dachsous complexes at junctions across the tissue axis from low to high Four-jointed
source: These results directly confirm the predictions of the model, showing not only that a slight gradient of binding strength exists across the tissue, but also that an opposing gradient of Ds phosphorylation usually acts to counter the effects of a gradient of Ft phosphorylation, resulting in a relatively even distribution of bound Ft–Ds complexes at junctions across the tissue axis from low to high Fj.
evidence: Supported by FRAP experiments and computational modeling

claim: The difference in levels of transcription between adjacent cells in a morphogen gradient may be very small (e.g., only a few percent or less of the peak expression levels)
source: A particular challenge for such a sensing mechanism is that the difference in levels of transcription between adjacent cells may be very small (e.g., only a few percent or less of the peak expression levels), and at the high end of the gradient this difference needs to be read against the background of a high overall expression level.
evidence: Based on general knowledge of morphogen gradients

claim: The asymmetric distribution of Fat-Dachsous dimers is a result of the patterns of transcription of the ds and fj genes as specified by upstream morphogens
source: Importantly, the asymmetric distribution of Ft–Ds dimers is a result of the patterns of transcription of the ds and fj genes as specified by upstream morphogens (Ambegaonkar et al., 2012; Bosveld et al., 2012; Brittle et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Four-jointed is expressed in a gradient, high at the putative distal end of the wing (the centre of the wing pouch) and low proximally towards the wing hinge in third instar wing imaginal discs
source: At this stage, Fj is expressed in a gradient, high at the putative distal end of the wing (i.e., the centre of the wing pouch) and low proximally towards the wing hinge (Strutt et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Dachsous is relatively uniformly expressed in the visible region of the wing pouch, but higher in hinge regions of the wing in third instar wing imaginal discs
source: whereas Ds is relatively uniformly expressed in the visible region of the wing pouch, but higher in hinge regions of the wing (Strutt and Strutt, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Much of the proximal wing blade is folded at the larval stage and most likely has high levels of Dachsous expression
source: It is important to point out that much of the proximal wing blade is folded at the larval stage and most likely also has high levels of Ds expression and this region of high Ds expression could therefore also be promoting Ft–Ds asymmetry.
evidence: Inferred from tissue morphology and expression patterns

claim: Boundaries of Dachsous expression may only be able to act as a patterning cue over a few cell diameters
source: Although we believe that both the Fj and Ds expression patterns are important cues for specifying Ft–Ds asymmetry in the wing pouch, the evidence suggests that boundaries of Ds expression may only be able to act as a patterning cue over a few cell diameters (Ambegaonkar et al., 2012; Brittle et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Throughout much of the wing pouch the Four-jointed gradient is likely to be a dominant cue for Fat-Dachsous asymmetry
source: and therefore throughout much of the wing pouch the Fj gradient is likely to be a dominant cue.
evidence: Inferred from limited range of Ds boundary effects and extent of Fj gradient

claim: Phosphorylation of Fat promotes its binding to Dachsous in vitro
source: In in vitro assays, Fj is able to mediate the phosphorylation of extracellular cadherin repeats of Ft and Ds, and phosphorylation of Ft has been shown to promote its binding to Ds, whereas phosphorylation of Ds appears to inhibit its binding to Ft (Ishikawa et al., 2008; Brittle et al., 2010; Simon et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous in vitro studies

claim: Phosphorylation of Dachsous inhibits its binding to Fat in vitro
source: In in vitro assays, Fj is able to mediate the phosphorylation of extracellular cadherin repeats of Ft and Ds, and phosphorylation of Ft has been shown to promote its binding to Ds, whereas phosphorylation of Ds appears to inhibit its binding to Ft (Ishikawa et al., 2008; Brittle et al., 2010; Simon et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous in vitro studies

claim: The gradient of Four-jointed in the wing pouch is predicted to produce opposing gradients of Fat–Dachsous binding affinities
source: Thus, the gradient of Fj in the wing pouch is predicted to produce opposing gradients of Ft–Ds binding affinities, with Ft–Ds binding favoured between cells moving down a Fj gradient, and Ds-Ft binding favoured between cells moving up a Fj gradient (Figure 6A).
evidence: Inferred from in vitro phosphorylation effects and Fj gradient

claim: Opposing binding gradients might play a role in producing uniform Fat–Dachsous interactions across the tissue
source: It has been previously proposed that these opposing binding gradients might play a role in producing uniform Ft–Ds interactions across the tissue (Simon et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: The effects of Four-jointed on Fat–Dachsous binding and the total amounts stably localised to cell junctions are relatively modest
source: An interesting experimental observation is that the effects of Fj on Ft–Ds binding and the total amounts stably localised to cell junctions are relatively modest.
evidence: Observed from experimental FRAP data

claim: Blocking the phosphorylation of either Fat or Dachsous only decreases the stable junctional amounts by about twofold
source: For instance, blocking the phosphorylation of either Ft or Ds only decreases the stable junctional amounts by about twofold.
evidence: Observed from phosphomutant FRAP experiments

claim: All molecular species (Ds, DsP, Ft, and FtP) contribute to the final population of bound Fat and Dachsous at cell junctions
source: Thus, all the molecular species (i.e., Ds and DsP and Ft and FtP) contribute to the final population of bound Ft and Ds at cell junctions.
evidence: Inferred from modest effects of blocking individual phosphorylation events

claim: The ability of the gradient of phosphorylated Dachsous to oppose the gradient of phosphorylated Fat is reduced due to the stronger effect of Four-jointed on Fat
source: A simple prediction of this observation, confirmed by our computational model, is that the ability of the gradient of phosphorylated Ds to oppose the gradient of phosphorylated Ft is reduced, and therefore a gradient of Ft–Ds binding is expected to be observed across the tissue (Figures 5A and 6A).
evidence: Predicted by computational model and confirmed experimentally

claim: The computational model results in relatively modest cellular asymmetries of Fat and Dachsous distributions (around 10% of the total cellular levels)
source: We note that our computational simulations result in relatively modest cellular asymmetries of Ft and Ds distributions (around 10% of the total cellular levels), whereas in vivo, observed Ds asymmetry can be as high as twofold (Ambegaonkar et al., 2012; Brittle et al., 2012).
evidence: Comparison of model predictions with experimental observations from cited studies

claim: In vivo, observed Dachsous asymmetry can be as high as twofold
source: We note that our computational simulations result in relatively modest cellular asymmetries of Ft and Ds distributions (around 10% of the total cellular levels), whereas in vivo, observed Ds asymmetry can be as high as twofold (Ambegaonkar et al., 2012; Brittle et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous experimental studies

claim: The computational model does not capture the full complexity of a three-dimensional cell environment and changes that occur in protein production and degradation and other cell properties over time
source: However, our model is only intended to make simple predictions regarding the effects of binding and redistribution of Ft and Ds molecules in a simple one-dimensional system and does not capture the full complexity of a three-dimensional cell environment and changes that occur in protein production and degradation and other cell properties over time.
evidence: Acknowledged limitation of the modeling approach

claim: Relatively weak asymmetries generated by expression gradients might be amplified by feedback mechanisms
source: Furthermore, it is generally believed that relatively weak asymmetries generated by expression gradients might subsequently be amplified by feedback mechanisms (Ambegaonkar et al., 2012; Brittle et al., 2012), and some molecular mechanisms that might contribute to amplification have recently been identified (Bosch et al., 2014; Rodrigues-Campos and Thompson, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: The majority of stable Fat–Dachsous at junctions is concentrated in bright regions referred to as puncta
source: With regard to possible amplification mechanisms, an intriguing observation is that the majority of stable Ft–Ds at junctions is concentrated in bright regions which we refer to as 'puncta'.
evidence: Observed from imaging and FRAP experiments

claim: Mobile junctional populations of Fat and Dachsous show reduced mobility within puncta regions
source: Furthermore, even mobile junctional populations of Ft and Ds show reduced mobility within these brighter regions.
evidence: Observed from FRAP rate analysis

claim: There may be cis-interactions between Fat and Dachsous molecules in cell junctions
source: This might suggest that in addition to trans-interactions between Ft and Ds in neighbouring cells, there may also be cis-interactions between Ft and Ds molecules in cell junctions, a view supported by previous experimental reports (Matakatsu and Blair, 2006; Sopko et al., 2009).
evidence: Speculative interpretation supported by citations to previous studies

claim: A clustering mechanism involving cis-interactions could provide the molecular basis of a positive feedback interaction
source: Such a clustering mechanism could provide the molecular basis of a positive feedback interaction.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of puncta formation

claim: Fat–Dachsous puncta do not co-localise with core planar polarity protein puncta at junctions
source: Previous observations have suggested that Ft–Ds puncta do not co-localise with 'core' planar polarity protein puncta at junctions (Ma et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: Fat-Dachsous puncta could correspond to specialised membrane domains that favour binding
source: We are unsure as to the reasons for these distinct puncta populations, they could correspond to specialised membrane domains that favour binding or they could be random regions of protein clustering driven by cis-dimerisation or cytoskeleton tethering.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of puncta nature

claim: Fat-Dachsous puncta could be random regions of protein clustering driven by cis-dimerisation or cytoskeleton tethering
source: We are unsure as to the reasons for these distinct puncta populations, they could correspond to specialised membrane domains that favour binding or they could be random regions of protein clustering driven by cis-dimerisation or cytoskeleton tethering.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of puncta nature

claim: Modification of analogous serine residues in cadherin repeats of Fat and Dachsous by Four-jointed phosphorylation leads to opposite effects on their binding activity
source: A final conundrum is the observation, first made in vitro, which we have now confirmed in vivo, that modification of analogous serine residues in cadherin repeats of Ft and Ds by Fj phosphorylation leads to opposite effects on their binding activity.
evidence: Confirmed by in vivo experiments building on previous in vitro observations

claim: Phosphorylation events may lead to changes in the intramolecular conformation of the extracellular regions of Fat and Dachsous
source: A possible working hypothesis is that phosphorylation events lead to changes in the intramolecular conformation of the extracellular regions of Ft and Ds, by analogy to the way in which phosphorylation frequently acts to cause other classes of molecules to enter 'open' or 'closed' conformations (Xu and Carpenter, 1999; Potter et al., 2005; Bertocchi et al., 2012).
evidence: Speculative hypothesis supported by citations to analogous mechanisms

claim: Phosphorylation of each molecule (Fat and Dachsous) may cause it to enter an open conformation, with open Fat binding most favourably to Dachsous and closed Dachsous binding most favourably to Fat
source: A possible scenario is that phosphorylation of each molecule causes it to enter an 'open' conformation, and that 'open' Ft binds most favourably to Ds, but 'closed' Ds binds most favourably to Ft (Figure 6B).
evidence: Speculative model illustrated in Figure 6B

claim: Mammalian Fat4 and Dachsous1 have multiple hairpin-like bends in their C-terminal regions caused by the loss of calcium binding linkers
source: A recent publication analysing the configuration of mammalian Ft4 and Ds1 revealed multiple hairpin-like bends in their C-terminal regions caused by the loss of calcium binding linkers (Tsukasaki et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent structural study

claim: Four-jointed phosphorylation may result in conformational changes between cadherin repeat domains near calcium binding sites resulting in the regulation of binding strength
source: It is possible that Fj phosphorylation results in conformational changes between cadherin repeat domains near to these calcium binding sites resulting in the regulation of binding strength, as suggested previously for E-cadherin (Petrova et al., 2012).
evidence: Speculative interpretation supported by citation to analogous mechanism in E-cadherin

claim: A hierarchy of binding affinities was used in the computational model, with phosphorylated Fat and unphosphorylated Dachsous producing the strongest partnership, and unphosphorylated Fat and phosphorylated Dachsous producing the weakest partnership
source: A hierarchy of binding affinities was used, based on the in vitro experiments (Brittle et al., 2010; Simon et al., 2010), with phosphorylated Ft (FtP) and unphosphorylated Ds (Ds) producing the strongest partnership, and unphosphorylated Ft (Ft) and phosphorylated Ds (DsP) producing the weakest partnership (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: Based on in vitro experimental results from cited studies

claim: Ft and Ds are allowed to redistribute in the computational model in accordance with experimental observations of protein mobility
source: We also allowed redistribution of Ft and Ds to occur in the model, in accordance with our experimental observations of protein mobility (see Figure 2C,D,L).
evidence: Model parameter based on experimental FRAP data

claim: In the computational model, Four-jointed is allowed to phosphorylate either Fat or Dachsous in proportion to its concentration
source: In the model, Fj is allowed to phosphorylate either Ft or Ds in proportion to its concentration, and Ft and Ds are then permitted to freely bind at cell edges until they reach equilibrium (see Figure 1A).
evidence: Description of model design

claim: In the computational model, Fat and Dachsous are permitted to freely bind at cell edges until they reach equilibrium
source: In the model, Fj is allowed to phosphorylate either Ft or Ds in proportion to its concentration, and Ft and Ds are then permitted to freely bind at cell edges until they reach equilibrium (see Figure 1A).
evidence: Description of model design

claim: The computational model reflects a one-dimensional line of cells each with two compartments to simulate Fat–Dachsous binding between cells according to a Four-jointed gradient
source: As an aid to understand the possible consequences for the generation of cellular asymmetry of Fj acting on either Ft or Ds or both, we generated a computational model reflecting a one-dimensional line of cells each with two compartments, to simulate Ft–Ds binding between cells according to a Fj gradient (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: Description of model design

claim: A Four-jointed gradient can lead to cellular asymmetry of Fat–Dachsous if Fj acts on either Ft or Ds or both
source: Using this we show that a Fj gradient can lead to cellular asymmetry of Ft–Ds if Fj acts on either Ft or Ds or both.
evidence: Demonstrated by computational modeling

claim: The predictions of the current model differ from a previous study which suggested that Four-jointed acting only on Fat would not result in a cellular asymmetry of activity
source: Our predictions differ from those of a previous study (Simon et al., 2010) which suggested that Fj acting only on Ft would not result in a cellular asymmetry of activity: the origin of this difference is that in our model (in accordance with our experimental observations) the Ft and Ds populations are mobile and able to redistribute to the most favourable cell edge.
evidence: Comparison with previous modeling study, explained by different model assumptions

claim: In the current model, the Fat and Dachsous populations are mobile and able to redistribute to the most favourable cell edge
source: Our predictions differ from those of a previous study (Simon et al., 2010) which suggested that Fj acting only on Ft would not result in a cellular asymmetry of activity: the origin of this difference is that in our model (in accordance with our experimental observations) the Ft and Ds populations are mobile and able to redistribute to the most favourable cell edge.
evidence: Model design based on experimental observations

claim: Only in the situation that Four-jointed acts on both Fat and Dachsous is the amount of Fat–Dachsous dimers bound at the junctions approximately the same across the entire axis of the Four-jointed gradient
source: However, in agreement with the same study, our model does predict that only in the situation that Fj acts on both Ft and Ds is the amount of Ft–Ds dimers bound at the junctions approximately the same across the entire axis of the Fj gradient.
evidence: Predicted by computational model, in agreement with previous study
